(c) General/knowledge prompts default to standard BPE. (b) Character/string segments → character-level tokenization with space-separated characters. (c) Code segments → character-level tokenization for identifiers and operators. (d) General/semantic segments → standard BPE (unchanged). Overhead is confined to pre-generation (<100ms).\n\n**Core Ablation Design (RQ1 — Mixed-Granularity Validation with Positional Analysis).** This is the paper's central empirical contribution. We measure per-segment accuracy independently (did arithmetic accuracy improve? did NL comprehension degrade?).\n\n*Positional encoding analysis (new).* We hypothesize that RoPE positional disruption is the primary risk for mixed-granularity tokenization. When a single BPE token (e.g., 'hello') is expanded into 5 character tokens, all downstream tokens shift by +4 position IDs, altering the rotary angles that govern every subsequent attention computation. This is directly analogous to the positional confusion observed in VLMs when image tokens shift text positions (Huang et al. 2025: 22-point DocVQA drops). We conduct three specific analyses: (a) **Position-ID shift measurement**: For each ablation condition, we compute the distribution of position-ID offsets between mixed and uniform tokenizations for semantically-corresponding tokens — quantifying how much positional 'drift' each condition introduces and how drift magnitude correlates with accuracy degradation. (b) **Attention pattern analysis at granularity boundaries**: We extract attention maps from the first 4 layers (where Word Recovery showed in-group character attention emerges) and compare attention entropy and alignment at three locations: within uniform BPE segments, within re-tokenized segments, and at the transition boundary between granularities. The hypothesis is that boundary attention patterns will show elevated entropy and reduced alignment compared to intra-segment patterns, and that the magnitude of this disruption predicts accuracy loss. (c) **RoPE frequency-band decomposition**: Following Hong et al. (arXiv:2410.08703), who showed ~60% of RoPE dimensions capture local (<2000 token) dependencies, we decompose attention contributions by frequency band (high-frequency local vs. low-frequency global) and test whether high-frequency dimensions — which are most sensitive to small position shifts — disproportionately degrade at granularity boundaries. This transforms the positional encoding concern from a potential reviewer objection into an analytical contribution: we provide the first empirical characterization of how RoPE handles heterogeneous token granularity.\n\n**CoT Ceiling Analysis (RQ2).** We run a pilot comparing: (a) prompt-only re-tokenization (our practical method), (b) oracle CoT re-tokenization using constrained decoding that forces digit-level/character-level tokens in arithmetic/string CoT steps (expensive but feasible using vocabulary masking during generation), (c) CoT self-conversion baseline where we prompt the model to re-express numbers in digit-separated format within its own chain-of-thought (inspired by Tokenization Counts' finding that L2R→R2L self-conversion recovers ~21 points, from 75.6% to ~97%, performing 'nearly as well' as the 97.8% R2L baseline). This honestly bounds the approach's ceiling and positions prompt-only as the practical sweet spot on a known tradeoff curve — if the oracle gains are modest, prompt-only is validated; if substantial, we identify the gap and propose CoT-prompting as a lightweight mitigation.\n\n**Classifier Reliability Analysis (RQ3).** We evaluate task detection on a held-out set of 2,000 diverse prompts (500 per category), reporting precision/recall per class. We then compute the *expected accuracy under classification error*: E[acc] = P(correct_class) × acc_optimal + P(false_positive) × acc_degraded + P(false_negative_to_BPE) × acc_BPE. Since false negatives default to BPE (no harm), the critical metric is false-positive rate for non-general categories. We target <5% FP rate, which bounds expected degradation to <1.2 points (5% × 24-point worst-case).\n\n**Evaluation benchmarks (revised).** Primary gain targets: (a) *Large-number arithmetic*: Broken Tokens' own 10-digit addition/subtraction evaluation (direct comparison), Arithmetic-Bench (scaling to 10-20 digit operations), GSM-Ranges (numerical robustness with perturbed scales). (b) *Character manipulation*: CharBench (175K-row comprehensive evaluation), SubTokenTest (tokenization-specific failures). (c) *Code*: HumanEval character-level variants. No-regression controls: GSM8K, MATH, MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag — explicitly positioned as *controls where we expect no gain and no degradation*, not as targets. This framing avoids the trap of claiming digit-aligned tokenization helps GSM8K (it won't, since these benchmarks use small numbers and are 90%+ saturated for target models).\n\n**Baselines:** (i) Standard BPE (default), (ii) Always character-level (Broken Tokens' uniform baseline), (iii) Always right-aligned digits, (iv) CharDC-style prompting (string tasks), (v) Oracle task selection (upper bound with ground-truth task labels), (vi) Oracle CoT re-tokenization (ceiling bound). ## Overview

CharBench is a comprehensive suite of evaluation tasks designed to systematically assess the performance of LLMs on character-level reasoning tasks in English, with separate tasks for assessing models' performance on positional understanding (indexing) and occurrence tracking (counting).

## Key Results

Evaluating a diverse range of leading open-weight and proprietary models on CharBench finds that it presents a significant challenge to modern LLMs, with average accuracies of 43.6% and 32.3% on some tasks. More specifically, CharBench contains over 40,000 stratified character-level questions, where state-of-the-art LLMs only reach average accuracies of 43.6% on first-occurrence indexing and 32.3% on last-occurrence, compared to more than 70% on token-level analogues.

## Task Design

Counting tasks assess an LLM's ability to determine character frequencies within strings, including counting the occurrences of a specific character and identifying the set of unique characters in a word. Indexing tasks evaluate positional understanding by requiring the model to locate the position (index) of either the first or last occurrence of a specified character within a string.

## Analysis of Tokenization

For counting tasks, tokenization properties are weakly correlated with correctness, while the length of the queried word and the actual character count play a more significant part. For tasks requiring intra-word positional understanding, performance is negatively correlated with the length of the token containing the queried character, suggesting that longer tokens obscure information on character position for LLMs.

## Publication

The paper "CHARBENCH: Evaluating the Role of Tokenization in Character-Level Tasks" by Uzan and Pinter (2026) was published in the Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (39 ed.) by the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence.

## RoPE's Core Limitations and Challenges

RoPE's pure sinusoidal structure can degrade when extrapolating far beyond the pretraining window, possibly exhibiting content-agnostic distance bias. Additionally, RoPE is not able to extrapolate to context lengths that were not seen during pretraining.

## Solutions and Extensions

Solutions include base-frequency scaling, position interpolation, and advanced extensions such as Token-Aware Phase Attention (TAPA), which injects learnable phase information and achieves uniform attention statistics at extreme lengths. Length-aware modifications (e.g., LaMPE, LARoPE) dynamically rescale or normalize RoPE's index usage, ameliorating out-of-distribution length degradation without retraining.

## Mixed Tokenization and Multimodal Challenges

A significant issue in 2025-2026 research addresses mixed tokenization scenarios. Naïve application of RoPE to multimodal inputs can induce spurious cross-modal positional biases, and research has introduced remedial encodings such as Circle-RoPE, MHRoPE/MRoPE-Interleave, and dual-frame fusions, which explicitly decouple text-image indices.

## Current Status in 2025-2026

For most language and multimodal workloads in 2025, RoPE delivers the best trade-off of simplicity, efficiency, and length-extrapolation, making it the default positional choice, despite the ongoing research into its refinements.

## Overview

This paper identifies intrinsic limitations of Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) in Transformer-based long-context language models.

## Key Findings

As context length increases, RoPE-based attention becomes unpredictable and loses two properties that are central to its effectiveness. First, it loses its locality bias: RoPE is no more likely to favor nearer positions than substantially farther ones.

The paper identifies two specific failure modes:

1. **Position Inversion**: As the context length grows, the same token may receive a higher attention score at a farther position than at a closer one, with probability approaching 0.5.

## Theoretical Analysis

The theoretical analysis abstracts away from the specific content of the context and depends only on its length. In both cases of failure, the probability of failure approaches 0.5, no better than random guessing. The attention score can remain unchanged when a key token is moved to a different position, or even replaced by a different token, indicating a failure to distinguish positions or tokens.

## Key Findings on Non-Canonical and Mixed Tokenization

Modern tokenizers employ deterministic algorithms to map text into a single "canonical" token sequence, yet the same string can be encoded as many noncanonical tokenizations using the tokenizer vocabulary.

### Model Robustness to Non-Canonical Tokenizations

Recent work investigates the robustness of language models to text encoded with non-canonical tokenizations entirely unseen during training, finding that instruction-tuned models retain up to 93.4% of their original performance when given a randomly sampled tokenization, and 90.8% with character-level tokenization.

### Performance Improvements Through Tokenization Strategies

Character-level segmentation improves string manipulation and code understanding tasks by up to +14%, and right-aligned digit grouping enhances large-number arithmetic by +33%.

### Understanding the Underlying Mechanism

The robustness arises in the instruction-tuning phase, with base models perceiving non-canonical tokenizations as containing misspellings and degenerating into nonsensical output, while post-trained models are committed to fluent responses.

### The Canonicality Problem

Although each string of text has one correct or canonical tokenization under BPE, current models can mistakenly assign probability to many invalid, noncanonical versions, wasting modeling power and potentially distorting the model's understanding of language through noncanonical hallucinations.

The research demonstrates that models are more flexible with tokenization than previously believed, and this flexibility can be leveraged at inference time to improve performance on specific tasks.

## Overview

zip2zip is a novel method for achieving context-adaptive tokenization in LLMs at inference time. It was published as a NeurIPS 2025 poster.

## How It Works

Leveraging an online data compression algorithm (Lempel–Ziv–Welch), zip2zip dynamically expands its active vocabulary at inference time by continuously replacing fragmented token sequences with more compact hypertokens, which it can immediately output during generation.

zip2zip consists of three key components: (1) a tokenizer based on Lempel–Ziv–Welch compression that incrementally merges co-occurring tokens into reusable hypertokens on the fly; (2) a dynamic embedding (and unembedding) layer that computes embeddings for newly formed hypertokens at runtime; and (3) a variant of autoregressive language modeling that pretrains the model to handle hypertokenized, compressed text sequences as inputs and outputs.

## Key Results

An existing LLM can be uptrained for zip2zip in 10 GPU-hours via parameter-efficient finetuning, reducing input and output tokens by 15–40%. The resulting zip2zip LLMs effectively learn to use hypertokens at inference time, reducing input and output sequence length by 20–60%, with significant improvements in inference latency.

Code and models are released at https://github.com/epfl-dlab/zip2zip.

ByteFlow Net is a new hierarchical architecture that removes tokenizers entirely and instead enables models to learn their own segmentation of raw byte streams into semantically meaningful units. I found the paper you're looking for! Here's what the research is about:

"Say Anything but This: When Tokenizer Betrays Reasoning in LLMs" is an arXiv paper by Navid Ayoobi and colleagues that examines how modern subword tokenizers produce non-unique encodings where multiple token ID sequences can detokenize to identical surface strings.

The work shows that tokenization can betray LLM reasoning through one-to-many token ID mappings. The researchers introduce a tokenization-consistency probe that requires models to replace designated target words in context while leaving all other content unchanged, and through analysis of over 11,000 replacement trials across state-of-the-art open-source LLMs, they find a non-trivial rate of outputs exhibit "phantom edits": cases where models operate under the illusion of correct reasoning, a phenomenon arising from tokenizer-induced representational defects.

They provide a taxonomy of eight systematic tokenizer artifacts, including whitespace-boundary shifts and intra-word resegmentation. The findings indicate that part of apparent reasoning deficiency originates in the tokenizer layer, motivating tokenizer-level remedies before incurring the cost of training ever-larger models.

The paper was published on January 21, 2026.
